name: Rafael Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, the high-voltage lines that carry power between cities. We travel, three weeks on and one week home, living out of a motel off whatever highway the line follows. A normal day is a long drive to the tower, harnesses on, and climbing a hundred and twenty feet to change insulators or string new conductor. I like the views and the crew. The motel food and the knees, not so much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home while you're away?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nobody, really. I'm single, I rent a one-bed near the depot that's empty half the month. My mum, Rosa, cleans offices downtown, and I send her money every month because her hours keep getting cut. I've got maybe four months saved, which is decent for me but it always feels like it's earmarked for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a lot of noise and some fancy emails. On the crew we'd joke about it at dinner, like, where's my robot to carry the come-along up the tower? I'd say the real story is still who owns the grid and who gets the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job's steady for the long run. The power companies are building more lines, not fewer, so there's always another tower somewhere. The worry I already carry is my mum, and AI going flat doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the rotation and take every extra job I'm offered while the money's good. I'd keep sending my mum her four hundred a month and try to add a little to my own savings. And I'd keep going to union meetings, because the next contract fight is about travel pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of flat, honestly. Not scared, not excited. It's just the life I've got, with the same holes in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum's hours keep getting cut. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cleaning company lost a big contract and they're squeezing everyone onto fewer hours. She's fifty-four and her back's bad, so she can't just go find something else. That's on me as much as on her now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long can you keep up three weeks on the road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five more years? The older guys say your body tells you when. My knees are already clicking on the cold mornings, and I'm twenty-seven. I'd like to move to a local distribution crew eventually, home every night.

say: AI is mostly **noise and fancy emails**, not a robot hauling gear up towers.
The real story is **who owns the grid** and who keeps the profits.
think: His job is **steady**, because they're building more lines, not fewer.
His real worry is his **mum's shrinking hours**, which AI doesn't touch.
do: Work the rotation and take **every extra job** while pay is good.
Keep sending his mum **four hundred a month** and save a little more.
Push the union on **travel pay** in the next contract.
feel: **Flat**, neither scared nor excited, carrying the same old worries.
S0.quote: The power companies are building more lines, not fewer, so there's always another tower somewhere.
fieldNote: His own job feels safe, but he carries his **mother's finances** too.
**Physical wear**, his knees at twenty-seven, is a quiet long-term pressure.
He frames everything through **ownership and profits**, not technology.

steps.text: Take every extra tower job on the rotation this year
Send his mum four hundred a month and save the rest
Back the union's push for better travel pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people the grid is about to get busier, not smaller. All those data centres running AI need power, so somebody has to build the lines to them. I'd post that the lineworkers are the ones keeping the AI boom running, so pay us like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine and I might even do well. The bit that worries me is the people around me: the clerks, my mum's office clients, the planners who used to know my name. When the work gets planned by software, the crew gets treated more like a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the data-centre build crews, because that's where the overtime will be. I'd save the extra and maybe finally get to six months. I'd also ask the union to make sure the new software can't push us past safe climbing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a bit hopeful. Funny how the AI that hurts other people could be the thing that keeps me busy on the towers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the office side of the transmission work change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the permits and the outage planning would go into a system. Right now a planner named Deb rings me and says the line's clear from Tuesday. Next it'll be a text from a program, and I'll miss Deb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for anything yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, like I do now, to translate a safety sheet or check a spec. I don't trust it to tell me a clearance distance, though. That I check in the book.

say: **Data centres** need power, so the grid gets busier, not smaller.
Lineworkers keep the AI boom running, so **pay us** like it.
think: He'll probably **do well** from the extra building work.
Software planning makes the crew feel **more like a number**.
do: Ask for **data-centre build crews** where the overtime will be.
Use the extra pay to reach **six months** of savings.
Push the union to cap **climbing hours** set by software.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, aware his gain comes alongside other people's loss.
S1.quote: Funny how the AI that hurts other people could be the thing that keeps me busy on the towers.
fieldNote: He sees **AI demand for power** as a boost to his own work.
His unease is mostly **for others**: planners, clerks, his mother's clients.
He uses AI **occasionally** but checks safety numbers in the book.

steps.text: Apply for the data-centre transmission build crews
Bank the extra overtime until six months are saved
Ask the union to cap software-set climbing hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and share the gains. Online I'd be the guy posting that if machines do the work, the hours should drop and the pay shouldn't. I'd be at the union hall arguing for a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got about three years and then I'm in trouble. By 2031 I'd be thirty-one, and a robot that climbs towers without a harness and never gets tired is exactly what a company wants for transmission. They'd keep a few of us to supervise, and I'm not sure I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop taking my savings for granted and push to get eight months put by. I'd ask the company about the robot programme early, before there's a queue, and try to get on the first trial crew. And I'd vote hard for anything that gives retraining money to trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the moment on a tower when the wind picks up and you realise you didn't clip in where you should have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking side changes in 2028, but towers need robots, around 2031. How does that split play out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work's gone in 2028 already, so the cleaning goes even thinner, and then by 2031 the cleaning robots. She'd need me more just as I've got less. I'd probably have to move her in with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your mum in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd want her near me, maybe we'd find a two-bed together and split it. It's not the life plan, but family is family.

say: If machines do the work, **hours should drop** and pay shouldn't.
He'd argue for a **shorter week** at the union hall.
think: He has about **three years** before tower robots arrive around 2031.
Only a few will **supervise robots**, and he may not be one.
do: Push savings to **eight months** in the first year.
Ask early to join the company's **first robot trial crew**.
Vote for **retraining money** for trades workers.
feel: **Anxious**, like realising on a windy tower he's not clipped in.
S2.quote: A robot that climbs towers without a harness and never gets tired is exactly what a company wants for transmission.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year lag** as a short window to get on the robot crews.
His mum becomes a **second, bigger** financial risk.
Steady adaptability shows: he'll **join early** but not lead.

steps.text: Grow savings to eight months of expenses this year
Sign up for the company's first robot trial crew
Vote for parties funding retraining for trades
Rent a two-bed and move his mum in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as before, but calmer. I'd say we've got time to bargain, so let's bargain properly: robot crews with a human lead, and nobody laid off without a year's retraining. I'd say that at the union and on the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me get ahead of the queue. I'd be thirty-four when the robots really arrive. If I'm already the guy who knows how to set up and check the drone stringing gear, I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone pilot licence in the first year, because drones already pull the pilot rope between towers. I'd learn the AI planning tools the office uses, even if I find them dull. And I'd keep saving, aiming for eight months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. There's a plan, there's a date. Still a knot in the stomach, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years until AGI and about eight until the robots. What changes with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than it did. If the robots come for transmission first, distribution might be safer for longer, with all the tight streets and trees. So maybe a local crew is the smart move, and I get my knees back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving to a local crew one day. Does that still make sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It also means I'd see my mum more. That's not nothing.

say: Bargain now for **robot crews** that always have a human lead in charge.
Nobody should be laid off without **a year's retraining** paid by the company.
think: Five years lets him **get ahead** of the queue for robot work.
He'd be **thirty-four** when robots fully arrive, still young enough to switch.
do: Get a **drone pilot licence** in the first year.
Learn the office's **AI planning tools** despite finding them dull.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, with a plan and a date.
S3.quote: If I'm already the guy who knows how to set up and check the drone stringing gear, I'm the one they keep.
fieldNote: More time makes him shift from fear to **positioning himself**.
He sees **distribution work** as safer for longer than transmission.
His mother stays central to every **life decision**.

steps.text: Get a drone pilot licence within the first year
Learn the AI outage-planning tools the office uses
Apply to move to a local distribution crew
Keep saving towards eight months by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this right, so no excuses. If the government and the companies don't plan a fair switch with ten years' warning, that's on them. I'd keep pushing the union line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly okay with this one. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when robots climb. That's long enough to move to a local crew, then into a supervising or training role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the move to a local crew in the next two years. I'd get the drone licence and then the robot operator course whenever the company runs one. And I'd help my mum save a little too, maybe a joint account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. It's a long runway. I've seen guys change careers in less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what's the difference between this and the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to make mistakes and fix them. With five, one bad call and you're out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay in the trade at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I think so. I'd want to be the old guy who teaches the robot crews where the bad trees are on the ridge. Somebody has to know that.

say: With **a decade's warning**, a fair switch has no excuses.
Companies and government own the job of **planning it**.
think: He'd be **forty** when robots climb, time to reach a supervising role.
Ten years lets him **fix mistakes**, unlike five.
do: Move to a **local crew** within two years.
Take the drone licence, then a **robot operator course**.
Open a **joint savings account** with his mum.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, seeing a long runway ahead.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the old guy who teaches the robot crews where the bad trees are on the ridge.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him feel **mostly in control**.
He values **local knowledge** as his lasting edge.
He'd stay in the trade, shifting to **training and supervising**.

steps.text: Move to a local distribution crew within two years
Take the robot operator course when the company offers it
Open a joint savings account with his mum

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years from now I'd have to be on a robot crew or out, and my mum would be losing work at the same time. What would help is the union winning retraining with pay, and some kind of support for people like her who can't retrain at fifty-four.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the travel. Half the guys on transmission crews are away from home most of the year. If robots take the road work, a few of us might actually get a life back. I'm not saying I want it, but I'm not saying I don't.

headlineQuote: If robots take the road work, a few of us might actually get a life back. I'm not saying I want it, but I'm not saying I don't.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **transmission lineworker** who travels three weeks in four.
He's single, rents a one-bed and **supports his mum**, an office cleaner losing hours.
He's pro-union and talks about **who owns the grid** before talking about machines.
He sees slow change as **good for his work** but fears tower robots by 2031.
With time, he'd move to a **local crew**, get a drone licence and supervise robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as he'd face tower robots while his mum loses work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** won by the union, plus support for older workers like his mum.
